abstract: Single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) intermediates arise during many DNA metabolic processes and are rapidly coated by the conserved ssDNA-binding protein Replication Protein A (RPA), which protects ssDNA and coordinates the recruitment of downstream DNA metabolic factors. However, how RPA directs the precise spatial recruitment of DNA metabolic proteins to RPA-coated DNA remains unclear. Here we show that RPA possesses an intrinsic preference for single-stranded/double-stranded DNA (ss/dsDNA) junctions, creating localized binding states that promote the junction-specific recruitment of incoming proteins. Junction-proximal RPA exhibits enhanced resistance to disassembly through conserved structural elements within its DNA-binding domains. RPA phosphorylation diminishes this junction preference, providing a mechanism for remodeling junction-associated complexes. We further demonstrate that RPA directly regulates the junction-specific loading and engagement of the nucleotide excision repair factor XPA. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic basis for RPA recognition of ss/dsDNA junctions and support a general framework in which RPA spatially organizes DNA metabolic factors at sites of ssDNA formation. More broadly, these findings resolve how proteins gain selective access to DNA embedded within RPA-coated intermediates and identify junction recognition as a previously unrecognized regulatory feature of RPA function.
